title: Speaking about Allah
hookLine: theology reasons about faith with arguments

cards: A king is arguing with Ibrahim about his Lord. Ibrahim says, my Lord is the one who gives life and causes death. The king says, I give life and cause death too.
So Ibrahim changes tack. Allah brings the sun up from the east, he says, so bring it up from the west. And the king, the Qur'an says, was left speechless.
That scene is in the second surah. It's not a sermon. It's an argument, made with reasons, against someone who disagrees.

teach.b: Today the path opens a new part, on the people who turned that way of talking about Allah into a whole discipline. First, the word. Kalam means speech, words.
The discipline is called 'ilm al-kalam, the science of speech, and its scholars are the mutakallimun, the ones who speak.
Writers give more than one reason for the name, but what it does is clear: kalam reasons about the articles of faith with arguments. Second, the license.
The Qur'an itself argues. Ibrahim argues with the king. Again and again it points to the heavens and the earth, to night and day, as signs for people who use their minds.
And it asks, in Pickthall's words, "Will they not then ponder on the Qur'an?" The mutakallimun took that as permission, even instruction, to think hard. Third, the questions.
The six articles raised things the list alone doesn't answer.
If Allah is one, how do His many names relate to Him? If everything is by decree, how is a person responsible? Is the Qur'an, Allah's speech, eternal or created?
Over the next days this path meets the schools that answered differently: the Mu'tazilah, the Ash'aris, the Maturidis, and their critics. Fourth, the critics.

Some scholars, notably in the Hanbali school, warned that arguing about Allah beyond what the texts say could pull people away from them. That caution is part of the story too. So kalam isn't faith replaced by reasoning.
It's faith asking questions out loud.

how: Islamic theology, 'ilm al-kalam, is taught in seminaries and universities alongside law and hadith, through classic creeds and their commentaries; some scholars, notably Hanbalis, have kept a cautious distance from it.

o: a debate that settles who belongs to Islam and who doesn't
Islamic theology: reasoning about faith with arguments
the recited words of the Qur'an, said aloud in prayer

s: the Qur'an contains arguments with people who disagree
Ibrahim's argument with the king in the second surah is one.
some, notably in the Hanbali school, warned against arguing beyond what the texts say.
it reasons about the articles of faith, asking the questions they raise.

games.q: you are Ibrahim. the king says, I give life and cause death too. what do you say?
o: say: Allah brings the sun from the east; so bring it from the west.
games.why: in the second surah Ibrahim changes tack with that challenge, and the king is left speechless: an argument made with reasons.

practice: Let a question come up that you've carried a while and never quite said: about God, about why things happen, about what a word in a prayer really means.

Don't reach for the answer; say the question to yourself clearly, in one sentence, then again, a little more exactly. If you pray, you can bring it with you into prayer; if not, let it sit beside you, asked.

wordCard.voice: Kalam. Speech; the name for Islamic theology, which reasons about the articles of faith with arguments. Its scholars are the mutakallimun. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: faith seeks understanding. Tomorrow, the first of the schools: the Mu'tazilah. Peace be with you.
